The result, from the head, is `D/pakK.pak`, ..., `D/pak1.pak`, `D/pak0.pak`, `D`: a game directory's archives are searched before its loose files, and higher-numbered archives before lower ones.

The archive scan stops at the first missing number: with `pak0.pak` and `pak2.pak` but no `pak1.pak`, `pak2.pak` is never loaded. With no `pak0.pak` the game directory has only its loose files. A missing archive is not an error, and neither is a missing game directory.
An archive that opens but fails to load (PAK-1, PAK-2) is fatal; it is not skipped.

Game directories are added in this order, each in front of the previous ones: `<base>/id1` always; `<base>/rogue` if `-rogue` is given; `<base>/hipnotic` if `-hipnotic` is given; `<base>/<value>` if `-game <value>` is given. The order does not depend on the order of the options on the command line, so with both `-rogue` and `-hipnotic`, `hipnotic` is searched before `rogue`.

The value of `-game` is appended to `<base>/` as given: it is not checked, and it may contain `/` or `..`. `-game` marks the game as modified (FS-4.3). `-game id1` adds `id1` a second time, which changes no lookup result.
The game directory the engine writes to (`com_gamedir`, used by `COM_WriteFile`) is the last directory added by FS-1.7.

`-path` discards the search path built by FS-1 and builds a new one from the arguments that follow it, up to the end or the first argument starting with `+` or `-`. Each is put at the head in turn, so the last one listed is searched first. `-path` with no such argument leaves the search path empty. It does not change the game directory of FS-1.9, and it marks the game as modified (FS-4.3).

A `-path` argument whose extension (FS-2.3) is exactly `pak` is loaded as an archive; if it cannot be opened, the engine stops with the fatal error `Couldn't load packfile: <argument>`. Any other argument is a directory, and it is not checked to exist.

A `-path` argument's extension is the text after the first `.` anywhere in it, at most 7 bytes, compared case-sensitively. So `mod/pak0.pak` is an archive, but `./id1/pak0.pak` (extension `/id1/pa`) and `id1/PAK1.PAK` (extension `PAK`) are directories.
With `-proghack`, a lookup of exactly `progs.dat` starts at the second element of the search path instead of the first. No other name is affected.

QuakeC Studio does not implement `-cachedir` (a deliberate divergence). In id's engine it copies loose files from the search path into a local cache directory and reads the copy; it is off unless asked for on every platform (`sys_win.c` sets `parms.cachedir = NULL`, and `sys_linux.c` has "caching is disabled by default, use -cachedir to enable"), and it exists to speed up installs on network drives, which is not a property of game data.
A lookup returns the file from the first element of the search path, from the head, that has it. Elements after that one are not consulted, and nothing is merged across elements.
An archive element has a name if one of its entries matches by PAK-3.1.
A directory element has a name if the file `<directory>/<name>` exists and can be opened for reading. The name is joined with a single `/` and not otherwise changed.

In the shareware game (FS-4.2), directory elements are skipped for any name that contains `/` or `\`; archive elements are not affected. A loose `progs.dat` is still found; a loose `maps/start.bsp` is not.
A name found nowhere is not an error at this level: the lookup reports no file, and the caller decides (`COM_LoadFile` returns `NULL`).

A found file's size is the entry's `filelen` for an archive, or the file's length for a directory. `COM_LoadFile` returns its bytes followed by one NUL byte that is not counted in the size, so text files can be parsed as C strings.

Names in directory elements, the archive names of FS-1.4 and the game directory names of FS-1.7 are matched ASCII case-insensitively on every OS. id's code leaves this to the host filesystem, so the answer differs by platform; this spec fixes the answer of the DOS and Windows reference builds, whose filesystems ignore case, so that an install copied from a CD (`ID1/PAK0.PAK`) or a mod made on Windows behaves the same on macOS and Linux. Archive entries stay case-sensitive (PAK-3.1).

A name that is absolute (starts with `/` or `\`, or a drive letter and `:`), or that has a `..` path component, never matches a directory element (a deliberate divergence). id's code joins it unchanged, so it can read files outside the game directory; QuakeC Studio confines reads to the install. Such a name still matches an archive entry with exactly that name (PAK-3.1).

QuakeC Studio puts no limit on path lengths (a deliberate divergence). id's engine builds search-path and archive paths in `MAX_OSPATH` (128-byte) buffers with `strcpy` and `sprintf`, which overflow, undefined, when the joined path is longer; the length depends on where the player installed the game, not on the game data.

QuakeC Studio puts no limit on the number of archives (a deliberate divergence). On Windows, id's engine has `MAX_HANDLES` 10 file handles, of which `findhandle` uses slots 1 to 9; every loaded archive holds one for the whole session, and running out is the fatal error `out of handles`. That is a limit of one host's file layer, not of the format.
Once the search path is built, the engine looks up `gfx/pop.lmp` by FS-3, with the shareware restriction of FS-3.4 off, so a loose `id1/gfx/pop.lmp` counts.

If `gfx/pop.lmp` is not found, the game is shareware. If it is found, its first 256 bytes, read as 128 big-endian 16-bit values, must equal the 128 values of the `pop` table in `common.c`; if they do, the game is registered, and if they do not, the engine stops with the fatal error `Corrupted data file.`. A `gfx/pop.lmp` shorter than 256 bytes is the same error: id's code compares whatever the short read left in its uninitialised buffer, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer as the mismatch.
A shareware game that is marked as modified (by PAK-4.2, `-game` or `-path`) stops with the fatal error `You must have the registered version to use modified games`.
After the check, FS-3.4 applies to every lookup in a shareware game and to none in a registered one.

A rerelease install is a base directory of its own: on Steam it is the `rerelease` folder inside the original install, and elsewhere (GOG's Quake Enhanced, Epic, Game Pass) it is the game's install folder. Its `id1` holds `pak0.pak` and no `pak1.pak`.

The rerelease's game directories (`id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1` and any others it ships) are searched by FS-1 and FS-3 unchanged, with the rerelease folder as the base directory and the expansion chosen by `-game`, as QuakeSpasm and vkQuake run them.

`QuakeEX.kpf` in the rerelease base directory is a zip archive (it holds the localization strings, such as `localization/loc_english.txt`, that the rerelease's progs and maps refer to). It is not an element of the search path: FS-3 never finds a file inside it.

QuakeC Studio does not model the KEX engine's per-user game directories (`Saved Games\Nightdive Studios\Quake`); the rerelease engine is a compile target only (ENG-8), and the search path is the one id's engine builds.

A code is `E` (error) or `W` (warning) and four digits. The first two digits are the group: `01` lexical, `02` declarations and types, `03` expressions and statements, `04` project, limits and fatal errors, `05` errors this compiler adds where id's `qcc` has undefined behaviour (QC-27). Warnings use the same groups.
A code is never reused for a different diagnostic. A diagnostic that no longer applies is withdrawn with its statement, and its code stays unassigned.

Every diagnostic has a primary span: the token the rule names, or, for errors id's `qcc` raises at its lookahead token, the construct the rule is about. id's own report is `<file>:<line>:<message>` with the line of QC-1.5; the vanilla profile's differential tests compare messages and codes, not lines.

For the errors id's `qcc` raises, the message is id's text, with `%s` and `%i` filled in as id does. The parser keeps going after an error with recovery of its own (LANG-2); the error limit and stop-at-first-file of QC-24 are id's behaviour, not requirements on this compiler.
`E0101` "EOF inside quote": the file ends inside a string literal (QC-6.3).
`E0102` "newline inside quote": a line break inside a string literal (QC-6.3).
`E0103` "Unknown escape char": a backslash followed by anything but `n` or `"` (QC-6.2).
`E0104` "Bad vector": a vector literal's third component is not followed by `'` (QC-5.2).
`E0105` "Unknown punctuation": a byte that starts no token (QC-7.2).
`E0106` "Unknown frame macro $NAME": a `$` word that is neither a known command nor a frame defined earlier in the file (QC-8.5, QC-8.8).
`E0107` "hanging $": `$` with no word after it on its line (QC-8.1).
`E0201` "not a name": a name was required (QC-3, QC-14.2, QC-4.5).
`E0202` "name too long": a name of 63 bytes or more, `LIMIT_QCC_MAX_NAME - 1` (QC-3.3).
`E0203` "\"TOKEN\" is not a type": a type was required (QC-10, QC-10.4).
`E0204` "expected X, found Y": the parser required the token X (QC-11.2, QC-14.6, QC-14.7, QC-4.2).
`E0205` "Type mismatch on redeclaration of NAME": a name redeclared with another type (QC-11.5, QC-12.3, QC-13.6).
`E0206` "NAME redeclared": a definition initialised twice (QC-11.5).
`E0207` "wrong immediate type for NAME": an initialiser of the wrong type, or any initialiser for an entity, void or field (QC-11.3).
`E0208` "Fields and functions must be global": a `local` field or function (QC-11.9).
`E0209` "Bad builtin immediate": `#` not followed by an integral float literal (QC-13.3).
`E0210` "state frame must be a number": a state function's frame is not a float literal or frame macro reference (QC-13.6).
`E0211` "function NAME was not defined": reported after all files for each global function never defined (QC-11.8, QC-24.6).
`E0301` "Unknown value \"NAME\"": a name with no definition in scope (QC-12.5).
`E0302` "type mismatch for OP": no row of the operator table matches the operand types (QC-16.2, QC-16.4); `OP` is the operator's spelling.
`E0303` "not a function": a call of something that is not a function (QC-18.1).
`E0304` "too many parameters": more arguments than a fixed parameter list (QC-18.1).
`E0305` "too few parameters": fewer arguments than a fixed parameter list (QC-18.1).
`E0306` "type mismatch on parm N": argument N, counting from 0, has the wrong type (QC-18.1).
`E0307` "More than eight parameters": nine or more arguments to a variadic function (QC-18.2).
`E0401` "No destination filename. qcc -help for info.": `progs.src` has no tokens (QC-23.5).
`E0402` "Error opening PATH: REASON": `progs.src` or a listed file cannot be read (QC-23.5).
`E0403` "compilation errors": compilation ended with errors (QC-24.6). It summarises and never stands alone.
`E0404` "bad parm order": a parameter resolved to a global below the previous parameter's offset (QC-13.5).
`E0405` "PrecacheSound: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS", "PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS" or "PrecacheFile: numfiles == MAX_FILES": a precache list is full (QC-26.4).
`E0501` "unterminated comment": a `/*` with no `*/`, at the `/*` (QC-27.2).
`E0502` "token too long": a name, string literal or other token longer than `QC_MAX_TOKEN - 1` bytes (QC-27.4).
`E0503` "`,` or `;` in a $frame list": on a `$frame` line (QC-27.5).
`E0504` "too many frames": more than `LIMIT_QCC_MAX_FRAMES` frames in one file (QC-27.5).
`E0505` "more than eight parameters in a function type" (QC-27.7).
`E0506` "initialiser is not a constant": a declaration initialiser that is not a literal or frame macro reference (QC-27.8).
`E0507` "builtin number must be positive": `#0` or `#-n` (QC-27.9).
`E0508` "cannot assign to this expression": the left side of `=` is a literal, a call, or an operator's result (QC-27.10).
`W0101` "frame name longer than 15 bytes; id's qcc cannot look it up" (QC-27.6).
`W0102` "macro NAME redefined" when a `#define` changes a macro's body (QC-9.3).
`W0201` "local NAME is the global NAME": a `local` or parameter whose name resolves to an earlier global (QC-12.3).
`W0202` "initialiser runs once, not on each call": a `local` with an initialiser (QC-11.10).
`W0301` "assigning to constant NAME": the left side of `=` is an initialised definition (QC-11.6, QC-27.10).
`W0302` "both calls return through the same global": an expression uses the results of two calls before either is stored (QC-18.6).
`W0303` "this call overwrites earlier arguments": a call inside an argument after the first (QC-18.5).
`W0304` "`=` binds tighter than `&&` and `||`": an unparenthesised `=` operand of `&&` or `||` (QC-15.3).
`W0305` "`!` applies to the whole comparison": `!` followed by an unparenthesised operand with a binary operator of priority 2 to 4 (QC-15.6).
`W0306` "`&` and `|` bind as tightly as `*`": `&` or `|` mixed with `+`, `-` or a comparison without parentheses (QC-15.2).
`W0307` "a vector condition tests only its x component" (QC-19.3).
`W0308` "return type does not match": `return e;` whose type differs from the function's return type, `return e;` in a `void` function, or `return;` in a non-`void` function (QC-13.8).
`W0309` "expression has no effect": an expression statement with no call and no assignment (QC-14.9).
`W0310` "`&&` and `||` evaluate both sides": the right operand of `&&` or `||` contains a call or assignment (QC-15.10).

`W0401` "exceeds a limit of id's qcc: LIMIT": the program needs more of one of `qcc`'s tables than it has (LIMIT-7.1, LIMIT-7.3), so it would not build reliably with id's `qcc`. This compiler is not bound by those limits.
`E0108` "unknown directive #NAME": a directive name the vanilla preprocessor does not know, outside a skipped block (QC-9.9).
`E0109` "#NAME without #ifdef or #ifndef": a `#else` or `#endif` with no open block (QC-9.6).
`E0110` "#ifdef or #ifndef without #endif": a block still open at the end of the file that opened it, at the directive that opened it (QC-9.6, QC-9.12).
`E0111` "cannot include PATH: REASON": an `#include` of a file that cannot be read (QC-9.11).
`E0112` "recursive #include of PATH": an `#include` of a file already being included (QC-9.11).
`E0113` "#include expects a file name in quotes" (QC-9.9).
`E0114` "#NAME expects a macro name": a `#define`, `#undef`, `#ifdef` or `#ifndef` without one (QC-9.9).
`E0115` "bad parameter list for macro NAME" (QC-9.9).
`E0116` "macro NAME expects N arguments, found M": a function-like macro use with the wrong argument count (QC-9.10).
`E0117` "unterminated argument list for macro NAME" (QC-9.10).
A source file is a sequence of bytes with no encoding. The text ends at the first NUL byte; anything after it is ignored.
Line numbers start at 1 and increase by one at each LF (0x0A) byte. CR (0x0D) is whitespace and never starts a line, so CRLF and LF files have the same line numbers.
Bytes 0x80 to 0xFF outside a string literal are whitespace. `PR_LexWhitespace` skips every byte whose `char` value is `<= ' '`, and `char` is signed on the x86 build, so these bytes are negative.
Bytes 0x80 to 0xFF inside a string literal are copied into the string unchanged.

The line number recorded for an emitted statement is the line of the token the lexer holds when the statement is emitted: the token after the last one the statement consumed. In `if (a)` followed by `{` on the next line, the `IFNOT` gets the line of `{`.
Whitespace is every byte from 0x01 to 0x20, plus the bytes in QC-1.3. It separates tokens and is otherwise ignored.

`//` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A `//` comment with no LF after it ends the file. (id's loop then steps past the terminating NUL and reads beyond the buffer; the reference build ends the file there, and this spec fixes that answer.)
`/*` starts a comment that ends at the first `*/` found by a scan that starts at the `*` of the `/*`. So `/*/` is a complete comment, and comments do not nest.
A `/*` comment with no closing `*/` stops one byte before the end of the file, and that last byte is then lexed as a token. QC-27.2 replaces this with an error.
Line breaks inside a comment count towards line numbers (QC-1.2).
A comment may stand between any two tokens, and between the components of a vector literal (QC-5.3). Inside a string literal, `//` and `/*` are text.
A name starts with an ASCII letter or `_` and continues with ASCII letters, digits and `_`. Case matters.

No name is reserved. The words `float`, `vector`, `string`, `entity`, `void`, `local`, `return`, `if`, `else`, `while` and `do` act as keywords only where the parser compares the current token with them: types at the start of a declaration or parameter, statement keywords at the start of a statement, `else` after an `if` statement and `while` after a `do` body. Anywhere else they are ordinary names, so `float do;` declares a global `do` and `a = do;` reads it, but a statement `do = 1;` starts a `do` loop.
A name of 63 bytes or more is an error, "name too long" (`PR_ParseName` tests `strlen(pr_token) >= MAX_NAME-1`). 62 bytes is accepted. LIMIT-7.2 states the same limit.

`PR_Check` and `PR_Expect` compare the text of the current token whatever its kind, and a string literal's text is its contents. So a string literal whose contents are a keyword or punctuation is taken as that keyword or punctuation wherever the parser checks for one: `"if" (a) b = 1;` compiles as an `if` statement. QC-27.3 diverges.
`for`, `break`, `continue`, `switch`, `case`, `goto`, `int`, `const` and every other word not in QC-3.2 have no meaning to vanilla `qcc`; they are names.
A float literal starts with a digit, or with `-` immediately followed by a digit, and continues over digits and `.` characters. Its value is C `atof` of that text, rounded to a 32-bit float.

A `-` immediately followed by a digit is always the start of a negative literal, whatever precedes it. `a-5` is the name `a` then the literal `-5`, which is an error ("expected ;, found -5" in a statement); `a - 5` and `a - -5` subtract.
`atof` stops at the second `.`, so `1.2.3` is one token whose value is 1.2.
There are no exponents, hex or suffixes: `1e5` is the literal `1` then the name `e5`. A literal cannot start with `.`: `.5` is the `.` operator then `5`.
There is no unary minus operator. `-` before anything but a digit is binary subtraction, so `a = -b;` is an error, "not a name"; id 1.01 writes `0 - b`.
A vector literal is `'`, three numbers, `'`. Each number is read as in QC-4.1, except that its first byte is taken whatever it is, so each component may be negative.
After each component the lexer skips whitespace and comments. If the byte after the third component is not `'`, it is an error, "Bad vector".
Whitespace (including line breaks) and comments may appear between the components and before the closing quote, and count towards line numbers.
A string literal is `"`, its contents, `"`. There is no concatenation of adjacent literals.
`\n` in the contents is one LF byte and `\"` is one `"` byte. A backslash followed by anything else, including a second backslash, is an error, "Unknown escape char".
A line break inside the literal is an error, "newline inside quote"; the end of the file inside it, or after its backslash, is an error, "EOF inside quote".
The contents are at most `QC_MAX_TOKEN - 1` bytes. id's lexer does not check and overruns `pr_token`; QC-27.4 makes a longer literal an error.

The punctuation tokens are, in the order the lexer tries them: `&&` `||` `<=` `>=` `==` `!=` `;` `,` `!` `*` `/` `(` `)` `-` `+` `=` `[` `]` `{` `}` `...` `.` `<` `>` `#` `&` `|`. The first one that matches the input wins, which is the longest match for every prefix pair in the list.

Any other byte that does not start a token (for example `%`, `^`, `~`, `?`, `:`, `@`, `\` or a backquote) is an error, "Unknown punctuation". The lexer does not advance past it, so recovery (QC-24.3) meets it again until the error limit stops the file.
`{` and `}` also adjust a brace depth that error recovery uses (QC-24.3).
There are no compound assignment, increment or decrement operators, no `%`, `^`, `~`, `?:`, shifts or comma operator. `qcc.h`: "There are no ++ / -- operators, or operate/assign operators."

`$` followed by a word starts a `$` command or a frame macro reference. The word runs from the first byte after `$` and any blanks to the next byte that is whitespace, `,` or `;`. `$` followed only by blanks before the end of the line is an error, "hanging $".

`$frame` defines frame macros: each word after it on the same line, split at whitespace, is appended to the file's frame list. The first frame defined in a file is 0, the next 1, and so on, across all `$frame` lines in the file.
The frame list is cleared at the start of each source file, so a frame macro is visible only in the file that defines it, after its `$frame` line.
`$cd`, `$origin`, `$base`, `$flags`, `$scale` and `$skin` are ignored with the rest of their line.

Any other `$word` is a frame macro reference. It becomes a float literal whose value is the index of the first frame in the list whose name equals the word; it can stand wherever a float literal can, including a global initialiser and a state function's frame (QC-13.6). A word not in the list is an error, "Unknown frame macro $word".
Because the word ends only at whitespace, `,` or `;`, a reference followed directly by another character includes it: `($b)` looks up `b)` and fails.
A frame name defined twice keeps its first index; the second definition still takes the next index, which no reference can reach.

`$modelname`, `$framegroupstart`, `$framegroupend`, `$load`, `$spritename` and `$type` (modelgen and spritegen commands that id 1.01's `models.qc` and `sprites.qc` use) are not `qcc` commands: they are references to undefined frame macros and fail as in QC-8.5. Those two files are not in id 1.01's `progs.src`. `$modelname` as FTEQCC reads it is part of the FTEQCC dialect spec (P2-01).

A `,` or `;` on a `$frame` line makes id's `qcc` loop forever appending empty names past the end of the frame table, and a frame name of 16 bytes or more overruns its slot into the next. QC-27.5 and QC-27.6 define what this compiler does.

A directive is a line, outside any comment, whose first non-blank byte is `#` followed, after optional blanks, by a name. A `#` anywhere else, or followed by anything but a name, is the `#` token. No program id's `qcc` accepts has a line that starts with `#` and a name, because a vanilla `#` is always followed by a number (QC-13.3), so the preprocessor changes nothing for vanilla code.

`#include "path"` replaces the directive with the contents of the named file, resolved relative to the directory of the file containing the directive. Diagnostics and statements in the included text carry the included file's name and lines.

`#define NAME` and `#define NAME text` define an object-like macro whose body is the rest of the line, trimmed. `#define NAME(a, b) text`, with the `(` directly after the name, defines a function-like macro. A later identical `#define` of the same name is accepted; a different one replaces the old one with a warning.

After its definition, a name token that matches a macro is replaced by its body, and a function-like macro's parameters in the body are replaced by the comma-separated arguments of the use. The replacement is rescanned for further macros, except the macro being expanded. Names inside string literals and comments are never replaced.
`#undef NAME` removes a macro; removing one that is not defined does nothing.

`#ifdef NAME` and `#ifndef NAME` start a conditional block that is kept when the name is (or is not) a defined macro. `#else` flips it and `#endif` closes it. Blocks nest; directives inside a skipped block are only counted for nesting. A `#else` or `#endif` without an open block, or a block still open at the end of the file, is an error.
Every token produced by expansion keeps the span of the macro use it came from, and the span of its text in the macro definition, so a diagnostic can point at both (LANG-1).
Macros and conditional state run on across the files of one `progs.src`, in compilation order (QC-23.3); frame macros do not (QC-8.3).

A directive name other than `include`, `define`, `undef`, `ifdef`, `ifndef`, `else` and `endif` is an error outside a skipped block, and so is a directive whose operand is missing or malformed: `#include` without a string literal, `#define`, `#undef`, `#ifdef` or `#ifndef` without a name, or a parameter list that is not names separated by `,` and closed by `)`. The directive line is then dropped. Tokens after the operand of `#include`, `#undef`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else` and `#endif` are ignored.

A function-like macro name not followed by `(` is an ordinary name and is not replaced. A use whose argument count differs from the parameter count, or whose argument list is not closed by `)` before the end of the file, is an error; the use is left unreplaced. Arguments are split at commas outside parentheses, and `F()` passes no arguments.
An `#include` of a file that cannot be read, or of a file that is already being included (directly or through other includes), is an error, and the directive is dropped.

A conditional block is closed in the file that opens it, whether that file is listed in `progs.src` or included. At the end of each file, every block it opened that is still open is reported (QC-9.6) and closed, so the next file starts outside it.
The simple types are `void`, `float`, `vector`, `string` and `entity`. A `vector` is three floats; every other type is one 32-bit word.
`.T` is the type of a field holding a `T`, for any type `T`, including a function type and another field type (`..float` is accepted).

`T(T1 n1, T2 n2, ...)` is the type of a function returning the simple type `T` with those parameters; `T()` takes none. A parameter's type may itself be a field or function type. The parameter names are part of the declaration, not the type (QC-13.2).
`T(...)` is a function taking any number of arguments of any types. `...` must be the whole parameter list: `void(float a, ...)` is an error, `"..." is not a type`.
A function type cannot return a function: after `T(...)` the type ends, so `void()()` is not a type.

Two function or field types are the same type when they have the same return or field type, the same parameter count and the same parameter types; parameter names do not matter (`PR_FindType` interns them).
A variable of type `void` may be declared; it occupies one word.
A function type with more than eight parameters is accepted by id's `qcc`, which writes past `parm_types[8]`; QC-27.7 makes it an error.
There is no `int`, array, struct, pointer or `const` type in the source language. The compiler uses a pointer type internally for field stores (QC-17.3).

A file is a sequence of declarations: a type, then one or more names separated by `,`, each optionally followed by `=` and an initialiser, then `;`. At file level there is nothing else: no statements and no stray `;`.

A declaration of a function type with an initialiser defines the function (QC-13). A function definition in a list is followed by `,` or `;` like any other name, so `void() a = {}, b = {};` defines two functions, and the `;` after a function body is required. `qcc.h`: "Don't forget the ; after the trailing brace of a function initialization."

Any other initialiser must be a single literal (or frame macro reference) whose type is exactly the declared type: a float, vector or string literal for `float`, `vector` or `string`. No initialiser is valid for `entity`, `void` or a field type; those are errors, "wrong immediate type for NAME".

id's `qcc` checks the initialiser's type against the type of the last literal the lexer read, without checking that the current token is a literal. So `float x = y;` after any earlier float literal is accepted and initialises `x` with that earlier literal's value, and the name `y` is consumed. QC-27.8 makes a non-literal initialiser an error.

An initialised declaration marks the definition initialised. A declaration of a name that already exists in scope with the same type refers to the same definition, so a name may be declared any number of times and initialised once. Declaring it with a different type is an error, "Type mismatch on redeclaration of NAME"; initialising it a second time is an error, "NAME redeclared".

An initialised global is a constant: its value is stored in the global area of the progs, it is not saved in saved games (QC-21.6), and literals of the same value reuse it (QC-20.2). Nothing stops code from assigning to it. `qcc.h`: "Anything that is initialized is assumed to be constant, and will have immediates folded into it. If you change the value, your program will malfunction."

Declaring a `vector` named `v` also declares `float` definitions `v_x`, `v_y` and `v_z` at its three words; declaring a field `.vector f` also declares `.float` fields `f_x`, `f_y` and `f_z` at its three field offsets. These are ordinary names (QC-15.7).

Every global function must be defined somewhere in the program; at the end of compilation each one that is not is reported, "function NAME was not defined", and compilation fails. A global of function type is therefore always a function, never a variable.
Fields and functions can only be declared at file level: `local .float f;` and `local void() g;` are errors, "Fields and functions must be global". Parameters of function type are allowed.

`local` declarations inside a function body have the same grammar as QC-11.1 and QC-11.3. A local initialiser is stored once in the progs' global area, like a global constant; it is not executed on each call, and later literals of the same value reuse the local (QC-20.2).
There are two scopes: global, and the function being defined. Blocks do not open scopes; a `local` anywhere in a function body is visible from its declaration to the end of the function.

All definitions, global and local, are kept in one list in declaration order. A name is looked up by walking that list from the start and taking the first definition with that name that is global or belongs to the current function.

A local or parameter cannot shadow a global declared before it: the lookup in `local float x;` or in the parameter `x` finds the global `x` first and reuses it (or reports a type mismatch if the types differ). Both then read and write the global.

A local of one function is invisible to every other function, so two functions may declare locals with the same name, and a global declared later may take a name that an earlier function used for a local.

Names are resolved when they are parsed: a function body sees only the definitions made before it in compilation order (QC-23.3). Using a name before any declaration is an error, "Unknown value \"NAME\"". `qcc.h`: "Source files are processed sequentially without dumping any state, so if a defs file is the first one processed, the definitions will be available to all other files."
The next-think name in a state function header is declared on the spot as a global `void()` when it does not exist yet (QC-13.6).
A function is defined by `= body`, `= [frame, next] body` or `= #number` on a declaration of function type. A body is `{`, zero or more statements, `}`; an empty body is allowed.

The parameter names used inside the body are the ones written in the type of the defining declaration. Names in prototypes are ignored. `qcc.h`: "The names are ignored except when the function is initialized."

`#n` makes the function the engine builtin number `n`: the function record's `first_statement` is `-n` and no statements are emitted. `n` must be a float literal with an integral value, else "Bad builtin immediate"; `#1.5` is rejected. Builtins allocate no parameter or local storage.

`#0` and negative numbers are accepted. `#0` leaves `first_statement` uninitialised in id's `qcc` (the reference build wrote 0), and `#-1` writes `first_statement` 1, a call to statement 1. QC-27.9 makes both errors.

Parameters are allocated first, in order, at consecutive global offsets; then the body's locals and temporaries as they are met (QC-21.4). If a parameter resolves to a global (QC-12.3) at a lower offset than the previous parameter, `qcc` stops with the fatal error "bad parm order".

In `= [frame, next] body`, `frame` must be a float literal or frame macro reference, else "state frame must be a number", and `next` a name, which is declared as a global `void()` if it does not exist and must have that type if it does ("Type mismatch on redeclaration of NAME"). The first statement of the function is then `STATE frame, next`. When it runs, the engine sets `self.nextthink` to `time + 0.1`, `self.frame` to `frame` and `self.think` to `next` (`OP_STATE` in `pr_exec.c`).
A body ends with a `DONE` statement after its last statement, so falling off the end returns.
Neither the return type nor the presence of a return value is checked: `return "x";` in a `float()` and `return;` in a `float()` both compile (`qcc.h` lists "return type checking" under TODO).

A function record holds `first_statement`, `parm_start` (the offset of its first parameter), `locals` (QC-21.4), the name and file as string offsets, `numparms` and each parameter's size in words. A variadic function's `numparms` is -1.
A statement is a block, `return`, `while`, `do`, `local`, `if` or an expression followed by `;`, chosen by the first token (QC-3.2).
A block `{ ... }` inside a function holds one or more statements. `{}` inside a body is an error ("not a name"), as is a lone `;`: there is no empty statement.
`return;` emits `RETURN` with no operand; `return e;` emits `RETURN e`.
`if (e) s` emits `IFNOT e, +n` jumping past `s`. `if (e) s1 else s2` emits `IFNOT e` jumping to `s2`, and a `GOTO` after `s1` jumping past `s2`. `else` binds to the nearest `if`.
`while (e) s` emits the condition, `IFNOT` past the loop, `s`, then a `GOTO` back to the first statement of the condition.
`do s while (e);` emits `s`, the condition, then `IF e` back to the first statement of `s`. The `;` is required.
The parentheses around an `if`, `while` or `do` condition are required.
There is no `for`, `switch`, `break`, `continue` or `goto`.
An expression statement may be any expression; one with no effect, such as `a;`, is accepted and its statements are emitted.
Binary operators have the priorities and associativity in the table below, tightest first.
`&` and `|` bind as tightly as `*` and `/`, so `b & c | 4` is `(b & c) | 4` and `a + b & c` is `a + (b & c)`.
`=` binds tighter than `&&` and `||`: `a = b && c` is `(a = b) && c`, and `a && b = c` is `a && (b = c)`.
`&&` and `||` have the same priority and associate left: `a || b && c` is `(a || b) && c`.
Comparisons associate left: `a == b == c` is `(a == b) == c`.
`!` is the only prefix operator. Its operand is an expression at priority 4, so `!a == b` is `!(a == b)` and `!a + b` is `!(a + b)`, while `!a && b` is `(!a) && b`.
A term is `!` expression, `(` expression `)`, a literal, a frame macro reference or a name. `v_x`, `v_y` and `v_z` are names (QC-11.7), not an operator.

The left operand of a call is the term or field access before `(`. A call ends the priority-1 loop, so neither `g().fl` nor `g()()` parses: `expected ;, found .`. Field access chains: `e.en.hp` is `(e.en).hp`.
Operands are evaluated left to right, and each operator's statement is emitted after both operands' statements; every operator result goes into a new temporary (QC-21.5).
`&&` and `||` evaluate both operands. `qcc.h`: "The && and || operators DO NOT EARLY OUT like C!"
The binary operators accept exactly the operand types in the table below and give its result types, emitting the named opcode.

There is no `vector / float`, no ordering of vectors, strings or entities, no equality of fields, and no `&&`, `||`, `&` or `|` on anything but floats: `if (e && a)` with an entity `e` is an error, "type mismatch for &&".
The same means the same type: two function operands of `==` must have the same function type (QC-10.6).
`!` accepts float, vector, string, entity and function operands and emits `NOT_F`, `NOT_V`, `NOT_S`, `NOT_ENT` or `NOT_FNC`; a field operand is an error, "type mismatch for !". The result is a float.

What the engine computes: `&` and `|` convert both floats to `int`, combine them and convert back (`OP_BITAND`, `OP_BITOR`); `&&` and `||` treat a float as true when it is not 0.0 (`OP_AND`, `OP_OR`); `NOT_V` is true when all three components are 0.0; `NOT_S` is true for the null string and for an empty string; `NOT_ENT` is true for the world entity; `EQ_S` compares string contents. The VM spec states the full rules.
A field access `e.f` reads the field `f` of entity `e`. On the left of `=` it becomes a store into the field (QC-17.3).

`x = e` requires `x` and `e` to have the same type and emits `STORE_F`, `STORE_V`, `STORE_S`, `STORE_ENT`, `STORE_FLD` or `STORE_FNC` with `e` as operand a and `x` as operand b. Its value is `e`, so `a = b = c` stores `c` into `b` and then `c` into `a`.

id's `qcc` does not check that the left side can be assigned: `5 = a;` stores into the literal's global, `f() = 3` into the return slot and `(a + b) = 3` into a temporary. QC-27.10 makes these errors.

When `=` is met and the last statement emitted so far is a `LOAD_*`, that statement is rewritten to `ADDRESS` (its result becomes a pointer to the field) and the assignment emits `STOREP_F`, `STOREP_V`, `STOREP_S`, `STOREP_ENT`, `STOREP_FLD` or `STOREP_FNC`, storing the right side through the pointer. This is how `e.f = x` stores into a field; in `e.en.hp = 3` only the last access becomes `ADDRESS`.

QC-17.3 looks at the last statement emitted, not at the left operand. If the previous statement ended with a field load and the next assignment's left side is a plain name, the earlier load is rewritten and the name's definition is retyped as a pointer: `e.fl; a = 2;` emits `ADDRESS e, fl, t` and `STOREP_F 2, a`. QC-27.11 diverges.
There are no compound assignments (QC-7.4).

`f(a1, ..., an)` requires `f` to have a function type, else "not a function". For a fixed parameter list, more arguments than parameters is an error, "too many parameters" (raised before the extra argument is parsed); fewer is "too few parameters"; an argument whose type is not exactly the parameter's is "type mismatch on parm N", counting from 0.
A variadic function (QC-10.4) takes up to eight arguments of any types; nine or more is an error, "More than eight parameters".

Each argument is evaluated and immediately copied to its parameter slot with `STORE_V` (three words, whatever its type), slot `i` being global offset `4 + 3i`. After the last argument, `CALLn f` is emitted, `n` the argument count.
The call's value is the global at offset 1 (`OFS_RETURN`), typed as the function's return type.

Because the slots are shared, a call inside a later argument overwrites the slots of earlier arguments: in `g(4, h(1))`, `h`'s argument is stored into slot 0 over the 4, so `g` receives 1. `qcc.h`: "afunc ( 4, bfunc(1,2,3)); will fail because there is a shared parameter marshaling area, which will cause the 1 from bfunc to overwrite the 4 allready placed in parm0."

Because the return slot is shared, two calls in one expression read the same slot after both calls: `g() + h()` adds `h()`'s result to itself. `qcc.h`: "total = factorial(3) + factorial(4); Will fail because the return value from functions is held in a single global area."
A call through a field, `e.th()`, loads the function from the field and calls the loaded value.

There are no implicit conversions and no casts. Every operand, argument and assigned value must have exactly the required type; the only exceptions are QC-19.2, QC-19.3 and the variadic arguments of QC-18.2.

The condition of `if`, `while` and `do` may have any type. The statement tests the first word of the value as a 32-bit integer (`if (!a->_int)` in `OP_IFNOT`): a float is false only when it is +0.0 (-0.0 is true), a string only when it is the null string, an entity only when it is the world, a function only when it is null.
A vector condition tests only its first word, the x component: `if (v)` emits `IFNOT v_x`, so `'0 0 1'` is false. `!v` tests all three (QC-16.5).
An empty string literal is not the null string: `if ("")` is true and `!""` is true (QC-16.5).
A `return` value is not converted or checked (QC-13.8); the engine copies three words from it into the return slot (`OP_RETURN`).
Every literal in an expression is a global holding its value. A string literal's text is copied into the string table and the global holds its offset.

Before allocating one, `qcc` walks all definitions in order and reuses the first initialised definition of the same type and equal value: a named constant, a local initialiser, or an earlier literal. Floats compare with `==`, vectors component by component with `==`, strings by the text at the definition's string offset.
Since `0.0 == -0.0`, `0` and `-0` share one global, holding whichever was met first.
A new literal's definition is named `IMMEDIATE`, is global, and is written to the global definitions table like any other definition (QC-25.3).
A string literal's text is copied into the string table once, when its global is allocated; a reused literal adds nothing.

A `string` declaration initialiser does not copy its text anywhere. The global receives the first word of the lexer's last literal value: the string offset of the last string literal allocated by QC-20.1, or the bits of the last float or vector literal read, whichever came last, and 0 (the empty string) before any. So `string s = "x";` gives `s` a wrong value, and no later `"x"` literal reuses it. id 1.01 declares no string constants. QC-27.12 diverges.
Global offsets 0 to 27 are reserved: 0 is null, 1 to 3 the return value, and 4 to 27 the eight three-word parameter slots. The first definition is at offset 28.

Every definition, temporary and literal takes the next free global offsets in the order the compiler meets them, its size from `QC_TYPE_SIZE`. A vector takes the three offsets of its `_x`, `_y` and `_z` definitions (QC-11.7).
A field definition's global holds its offset in the entity, in words. Field offsets are assigned from 0 in declaration order, a `.vector` taking three; the total is the progs' `entityfields`.

A function's `parm_start` is the offset of its first parameter and its `locals` count is the number of words from there to the end of the last `local` declaration in its body, including any temporaries allocated before that declaration; temporaries after the last `local` are not counted. A function with no `local` declaration has `locals` 0 even when it has parameters: 26 functions of id 1.01 do, `SUB_AttackFinished` among them.
Each operator, comparison or field load gets a new temporary that is never reused, not even across statements. Assignments, `IF`, `IFNOT`, `GOTO`, `RETURN`, `STATE` and calls get none.

A global definition is marked to be saved in saved games (`DEF_SAVEGLOBGAL`) when it is global, not initialised, and not a function or field. `qcc.h`: "All uninitialized globals will be saved to savegame files."
Each construct emits exactly the progs statements in the table below, in that order.
Branch operands are relative statement counts: `IF` and `IFNOT` carry the offset in operand b and `GOTO` in operand a, and the engine adds it to the index of the branch statement itself.
Operands a, b and c are signed 16-bit global offsets in the progs, as `dstatement_t` declares them; an unused operand is 0.
`qcc` reads `progs.src` from the current directory, or from the directory given with `-src`. It is a list of tokens: the first names the output file and each later one a source file.

Tokens are split as `COM_Parse` does: whitespace separates them; `//` starts a comment to the end of the line; `"..."` is one token without the quotes; each of `{`, `}`, `(`, `)`, `'` and `:` is a token of its own and ends a word. There are no `/* */` comments.
The source files are compiled in the order listed, as one program: each sees every definition of the files before it (QC-12.5). A file may be listed twice and is then compiled twice.
The output path is used as written, relative to the current directory, not to the `-src` directory; source paths are prefixed with the `-src` directory. id 1.01's `progs.src` names `../progs.dat`.
An empty `progs.src` is fatal, `No destination filename. qcc -help for info.` (with two spaces). A source file that cannot be opened is fatal.
Files that are in the source directory but not in `progs.src` are not part of the program (id 1.01 ships `amtest.qc`, `jctest.qc`, `models.qc` and `sprites.qc` this way).
id's `qcc` has no warnings. Every diagnostic is an error, printed as `<file>:<line>:<message>` with the line of QC-1.5.
An error abandons the current top-level declaration. Recovery then skips tokens until it consumes a `;` at brace depth 0 and resumes parsing declarations after it.
Recovery re-lexes from the error position, so a lexical error can repeat; an unknown byte (QC-7.2) repeats until the error limit.
The error count runs across the whole compilation. When the 11th error is reported, the current file stops.
After a file that had any error, `qcc` exits with status 1 without compiling the remaining files.
After all files, every global function that was never defined is reported (QC-11.8) and compilation fails with the fatal error "compilation errors".

An error raised while lexing the first token of a file happens before the recovery point is set up; id's `qcc` jumps through an uninitialised `jmp_buf` and crashes. QC-27.1 makes it an ordinary error.
The output is a version 6 `progs.dat`. Statement 0, function 0, global definition 0, field definition 0 and string offset 0 (the empty string) are placeholders written before anything compiled.
Functions are numbered in the order their definitions finish parsing, from 1.

The global definitions table has one entry for every definition, in declaration order: globals, locals, parameters, `_x`/`_y`/`_z` components and `IMMEDIATE` literals, but not temporaries. Field definitions appear in both the field table (with the field's type) and the global table (with type field).

Strings are appended to the string table as they are met, never shared: each source file's name when the file starts, each string literal's text when its global is allocated, and each function's name when its definition finishes. Then, while writing, the name of every definition is appended once for the global table and once more for each field definition's entry in the field table. The table's length is rounded up to a multiple of 4.

`qcc` also writes `progdefs.h` in the current directory: a C `globalvars_t` with every global declared before the one named `end_sys_globals`, and an `entvars_t` with every field declared before the one named `end_sys_fields`, each element typed by its QuakeC type.

The progs header's `crc` is the 16-bit CRC (CCITT polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF, no final xor) of the text of `progdefs.h` up to the `#define` line, with LF line ends, as `qcc` reads it back. The engine refuses a progs whose CRC differs from its own `PROGHEADER_CRC`, 5927 for id's 1.01 system definitions (`PR_LoadProgs` in `WinQuake/pr_edict.c`: "progs.dat system vars have been modified, progdefs.h is out of date").

Writing `progdefs.h`, `qcc` assumes every vector definition before `end_sys_globals` is followed by its three component definitions. A vector literal (an `IMMEDIATE` with no components) before `end_sys_globals`, or the absence of `end_sys_globals` with any vector literal, makes it read past the end of the definition list; the reference build crashed. QC-27.13 diverges.

When the called function's name starts with `precache_sound`, `precache_model` or `precache_file`, the compile-time string value of the first argument's global is added to that list, once per distinct string.
The byte after the prefix chooses the pak block: `1` to `9` give that number (`precache_sound2` is block 2), anything else block 1.
A first argument that is not a constant adds the string at its global's compile-time value, normally the empty string.
`PrecacheModel` checks the sound count, not the model count, against its limit ("PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS"), so the model list itself is unchecked.
A lexical error in the first token of a file is an ordinary error (QC-24.7).
A `/*` comment with no `*/` is an error, "unterminated comment", at the line of the `/*` (QC-2.4).
Keywords and punctuation are matched only against name and punctuation tokens; a string literal is always a string (QC-3.4).
A name, string literal or other token longer than `QC_MAX_TOKEN - 1` bytes is an error (QC-6.4).
A `,` or `;` on a `$frame` line is an error, and more than `LIMIT_QCC_MAX_FRAMES` frames in one file is an error (QC-8.9).
A frame name longer than `QC_MAX_FRAME_NAME` bytes is accepted and looked up by its full name, with a warning that id's `qcc` cannot use it (QC-8.9).
A function type with more than `LIMIT_MAX_PARMS` parameters is an error (QC-10.8).
An initialiser that is not a literal or frame macro reference is an error, "initialiser is not a constant" (QC-11.4).
`#0` and negative builtin numbers are errors (QC-13.4).

The left side of `=` must be a name or a field access; a literal, a call or an operator's result is an error, "cannot assign to this expression" (QC-17.2). Assigning to an initialised definition stays legal, as in id, with a warning (QC-11.6).
Only a field access on the left of `=` is turned into an address; an earlier statement's field load is never rewritten (QC-17.4).
A `string` initialiser stores the offset of its own text in the string table (QC-20.6).
`progdefs.h` generation skips component definitions only for vectors that have them (QC-25.7).

A `,` or `;` on a `$cd`, `$origin`, `$base`, `$flags`, `$scale` or `$skin` line makes id's `qcc` loop forever, as on a `$frame` line (QC-8.9). This compiler ignores the whole rest of such a line, `,` and `;` included (QC-8.4).
A version 6 statement operand is a signed 16-bit value, so a statement can name global slots 0 to 32767 only (PROGS-7.2); a program with more globals cannot reach the rest from code.
A definition's `ofs` is unsigned 16-bit, so a definition can name global or field slots 0 to 65535 (PROGS-9.2).
A definition's type has 15 bits once `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is removed: 0 to 32767.

A function has at most 8 parameters (`parm_size` has 8 entries and the call opcodes are `OP_CALL0` to `OP_CALL8`). Each parameter has 3 slots in the call area (PROGS-18.1), and qcc writes a `parm_size` of 1 or 3; the engine copies whatever `parm_size` says without checking it.

Entering a QC function adds one to the call depth, and the entry that makes the depth reach 32 fails with `stack overflow`. The function the engine calls counts, so at most 31 QC functions can be active at once.
The depth is shared by every QC function active in the engine, including those started by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` (for example a touch function run from inside a builtin).
Builtins do not count: calling a builtin does not enter a QC frame.

Entering a QC function saves its `locals` slots on a stack of 2048 slots shared by all active functions. An entry is allowed when the slots in use plus the new function's `locals` is at most 2048, and fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow` when it is more.

Each call of `PR_ExecuteProgram` has its own counter starting at 100000. The counter drops by one before each statement, and the statement that brings it to 0 fails with `runaway loop error` without executing, so one call executes at most 99999 statements.
Statements run by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` count against the nested call's own counter, not the outer one.
id's builtin table has 79 entries, numbers 0 to 78. Calling a function whose builtin number is 79 or more fails with `Bad builtin call number`.
Builtin 0 cannot be called: a `first_statement` of 0 is not negative, so the function runs statement 0 instead (PROGS-10.2).
A `first_statement` of -2147483648 has no positive builtin number; negating it overflows, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer as `Bad builtin call number`.

A server has at most 600 edicts, counting the world and the client edicts. When none can be reused and 600 are in use, allocating one (`spawn`, or an entity of the map being loaded) fails with `ED_Alloc: no free edicts`. Reuse rules are in `edicts.md` (P1-03).

The sound and model precache lists have 256 entries each, and entry 0 is always the empty string. Precaching a name already in the list does nothing; precaching a new name when all 256 entries are used fails with `PF_precache_sound: overflow` or `PF_precache_model: overflow`. So at most 255 sounds can be precached, and at most 255 models including the world model in entry 1 and its submodels after it.

qcc never checks its table sizes: more than 500000 bytes of strings, 65536 statements, 8192 functions, 16384 global definitions, 1024 field definitions or 16384 global slots overruns a fixed array, which is undefined in C. The result is not specified; a program that exceeds one does not build reliably with id's qcc.
A name of 63 or more characters fails with `name too long`, so a name has at most 62 characters.

qcc records the files named in `precache_sound`, `precache_model` and `precache_file` calls, 1024 of each. A new sound when 1024 are recorded fails with `PrecacheSound: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`, and a new file when 1024 are recorded with `PrecacheFile: numfiles == MAX_FILES`. For models qcc tests the sound count instead (`PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`), so a new model fails only when 1024 sounds are recorded, and the 1025th model overruns its array.
A PAK file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `PACK` (0x50 0x41 0x43 0x4B), then `dirofs` and `dirlen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `PACK` (the comparison is case-sensitive, so `pack` fails), loading fails with the error `<path> is not a packfile`. In id's engine this is a fatal `Sys_Error`.

A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code does not check the length of the read and decodes whatever was in the uninitialised header struct, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error, the same as PAK-1.2, because no valid archive is that short.
A PAK path that cannot be opened is not an error of the format: `COM_LoadPackFile` returns `NULL` and its caller decides what that means (FS-1.5, FS-2.2).
The directory is `dirlen` bytes at offset `dirofs`, holding 64-byte entries: a 56-byte name, then `filepos` and `filelen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.
The number of entries is `dirlen` divided by 64, rounded down. The remaining `dirlen % 64` bytes are not an entry; they are still read, and they count towards the CRC of PAK-4.1.
A `dirlen` from 0 to 63 gives an archive with no entries, which loads without error.
More than 2048 entries fails with the error `<path> has <n> files` (fatal in id's engine), where `<n>` is the computed entry count. Exactly 2048 entries loads.

A negative `dirlen` fails as PAK-2.4. The engine divides `dirlen` as an unsigned 32-bit value on the reference build, so any negative `dirlen` gives at least 33,554,432 entries; `dirlen` = -64 gives `has 67108863 files`. (A 64-bit build gets a different, also failing, result; the 32-bit answer is the one fixed here.)

A `dirlen` from 131,073 to 131,135 (2048 whole entries plus part of another) fails to load. id's code computes 2048 entries, passes the limit check and then reads `dirlen` bytes into a 131,072-byte stack array, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because the C overflows its buffer.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `dirofs`, or `dirofs + dirlen` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check the seek or the length of the read and parses uninitialised stack memory, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
An entry's name is the bytes of its 56-byte field before the first NUL. Bytes after that NUL are ignored.

An entry whose 56-byte name field contains no NUL fails the load. id's `strcpy` runs on into `filepos`, `filelen` and the next entries, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because no tool writes such a name and no single answer matches the C.

Names are kept as raw bytes: no case folding, no conversion between `/` and `\`, no trimming. `MAPS/E1M1.BSP` and `maps/e1m1.bsp` are two different names. An entry whose first name byte is NUL has the empty name.
Entries keep their directory order, and two entries may have the same name; loading neither merges nor rejects them.
`filepos` and `filelen` are not checked when the archive is loaded, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed (PAK-3.4 covers reading such an entry).
Looking up a name in an archive returns the first entry, in directory order, whose name is byte-for-byte equal to it. The comparison is case-sensitive and does not normalise separators.
An entry's contents are the `filelen` bytes starting at offset `filepos` of the PAK file. Entries may overlap each other, the header or the directory; nothing checks it.
An entry with `filelen` 0 has empty contents.

Reading an entry whose range does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `filepos` or `filelen`, or `filepos + filelen` past the end) is an error. id's code either fails in `Hunk_AllocName` (`Hunk_Alloc: bad size` for `filelen` below -1), writes before its buffer (`filelen` = -1) or returns the short read's uninitialised bytes; this spec fixes the answer as an error. The entry is still listed (PAK-2.12).

The directory CRC is CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021, not reflected, initial value 0xFFFF and no final XOR, computed over all `dirlen` bytes of the directory as they are in the file (before byte swapping, and including any partial entry from PAK-2.2). The CRC of an empty directory is 0xFFFF (65535).

An archive whose entry count is not 339 or whose directory CRC is not 32981 marks the game as modified. The check runs on every archive loaded, not only `pak0.pak`, and it never stops an archive from loading.

The rerelease's `pak0.pak` archives (in `id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1` and the other game directories of FS-5.2) are PAK archives as described by PAK-1 to PAK-3, each with at most 2048 entries, and need no extension of the format. This statement rests on QuakeSpasm's evidence above; it is confirmed against a real install by the reader's acceptance test in [#42](https://github.com/quakecstudio/editor/issues/42), because no rerelease data is available to CI (LIC-4).
Every multi-byte integer and float in the file is little-endian. The engine converts with `LittleLong` and `LittleShort` after loading, so a big-endian host reads the same values.

The file starts with the 60-byte header (PROGS-2) at offset 0. Each of the six tables (statements, global definitions, field definitions, functions, strings, globals) is located only by its offset and count in the header; the engine does not require any order, alignment, gap or absence of overlap between them.

id's qcc writes the tables in this order, each directly after the previous one: header, strings, statements, functions, global definitions, field definitions, globals. It pads the string table with NUL bytes to a multiple of 4, so every table starts 4-byte aligned.
Bytes in the file that no table covers are ignored, except by the file CRC (PROGS-6.1).

The first record of the statements, functions, global definitions and field definitions tables, and the first byte of the string table, are reserved: qcc writes them as all zero bytes (`InitData` starts every count at 1). The engine does not check them.
The header is 15 consecutive `i32` fields, 60 bytes:

Every offset is measured from the first byte of the file. A table occupies `count * record size` bytes from its offset; for the string table the count is already in bytes and for the globals the record size is 4.
The fields are signed in id's struct. The engine never compares an offset or a count with the file size and never checks a sign; a reader's checks are in PROGS-15.
A file whose `version` is not 6 is rejected with `progs.dat has wrong version number (<version> should be 6)`.
A file whose `crc` is not 5927 is rejected with `progs.dat system vars have been modified, progdefs.h is out of date`.
The version is checked before the CRC: a file wrong in both reports the version.
A field definition whose `type` has bit 15 (`DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) set is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: pr_fielddefs[i].type & DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`. The same bit in a global definition is accepted (PROGS-9.3).

These three are the only checks the engine makes on a loaded file; it does not check offsets, counts, string references, opcodes or operands at load. A missing file is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: couldn't load progs.dat`.

The header CRC identifies the system globals and fields a mod declares (PROGS-5), not the file: two different mods with the same system definitions carry the same value, 5927 for the definitions in id's `defs.qc`.

The CRC is the 16-bit, non-reflected CRC with polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF and final XOR 0x0000 (CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE). Each byte updates it as `crc = (crc << 8) ^ table[(crc >> 8) ^ byte]`, truncated to 16 bits, where `table[i]` is the CRC of the single byte `i` with a zero initial value.
The CRC of no bytes is 0xFFFF (65535), and the CRC of the ASCII bytes `123456789` is 0x29B1.
The header `crc` is PROGS-4's CRC of exactly that text, with `\n` as one byte 0x0A. For `WinQuake/progdefs.q1` it is 5927.
qcc stores the CRC zero-extended from 16 bits, so the field is between 0 and 65535 in any file id's qcc writes.
While loading, the engine also computes PROGS-4's CRC over every byte of the file as stored, before any byte swapping, into `pr_crc`.
`pr_crc` is never checked. Its only use is the server info message, which prints it as `VERSION <version> SERVER (<pr_crc> CRC)`.
A statement is 8 bytes:

The operands are signed 16-bit: the bytes `ff ff` are -1, not 65535. Most opcodes use an operand as a global slot index; `OP_GOTO` uses `a`, and `OP_IF` and `OP_IFNOT` use `b`, as a jump relative to the statement. Their meaning per opcode is in `vm.md`.
Statement 0 is reserved (PROGS-1.5); a function's code starts at `first_statement` (PROGS-10) and the table has no other structure.
The engine does not check `op` or the operands at load. An opcode above `OP_BITOR` (65) fails only when executed, with `Bad opcode <op>`.
The vanilla opcodes are numbered from 0 in this order, 66 in all (0 to 65):
A definition is 8 bytes:
`ofs` is unsigned: a definition can name any slot from 0 to 65535, unlike a statement operand (PROGS-7.2).

In a global definition, `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` marks a global that a saved game stores. qcc sets it on every global that has no initial value, is not a function or field, and is not a local or parameter. The engine strips the bit before using the type.
Several definitions can name the same slot: qcc gives a vector `v` the definitions `v` (vector) and `v_x` (float) at the same slot, and `v_y` and `v_z` at the next two.

For a field `.T name`, qcc writes a field definition with type `T` at the field's slot, and a global definition with type field (5) for a global slot whose value is that field slot index. A vector field also gets `name_x`, `name_y` and `name_z` field definitions and globals for its three slots.
Lookups by name compare bytes exactly (`strcmp`) and take the first matching definition in table order; lookups by slot take the first definition whose `ofs` matches.

qcc also writes global definitions for the parameters and locals of functions, without `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`, and one named `IMMEDIATE` for every constant slot it allocates (string, float and vector literals), so names in the table are not unique.
A function is 36 bytes:

A function with `first_statement` below zero is builtin number `-first_statement`; qcc writes `#25` as -25. The engine calls the builtin without reading `parm_start`, `locals`, `numparms` or `parm_size`.
A global of type function holds an index into this table, and index 0 is the null function: calling it fails with `NULL function`.
`parm_size` is eight single bytes and is not byte-swapped; entries at or past `numparms` are ignored (qcc writes them as 0).

`numparms` below zero copies no parameters; qcc writes -1 for a function declared with `...`. qcc does not limit the count to 8, but the engine reads only `parm_size[0..numparms)`, so a reader rejects more than 8 (PROGS-15.6).
The engine does not interpret `profile` at load; it adds one for every statement the function executes, starting from the stored value. qcc writes 0.

The string table is `numstrings` bytes holding NUL-terminated strings. A string reference (`s_name`, `s_file`, or the value of a string global) is a byte offset from the start of the table, and the string runs to the next NUL byte.
Offset 0 is the empty string: qcc writes a NUL as the first byte.

A reference may point into the middle of another string; the string is the bytes from that offset to the next NUL. qcc's `CopyString` appends every string it is given without looking for an earlier copy, so the same text can appear several times.
The bytes are uninterpreted: any value from 0x01 to 0xFF can be part of a string, including control characters and Quake's high-bit characters.
The table ends with zero to three NUL padding bytes from qcc (PROGS-1.3).

At run time a string value can also point outside the table, at strings the engine allocates (`ED_NewString`, `sv.name`); those values are still offsets from the start of the table and never appear in a file as written by qcc.

The globals are `numglobals` 4-byte slots holding the initial value of every global, constant and temporary. The engine executes in this memory directly, so the values in the file are the state before the first function runs.
A slot holds whichever type the code using it says (PROGS-17): the file does not tag slots with types, and only the definitions (PROGS-9) say what a named slot holds.
Slots 0 to 27 are the reserved return and parameter area (PROGS-18). qcc allocates every other global from slot 28 upward, so a file from qcc has at least 28 slots.
`entityfields` is the number of 4-byte field slots in every entity. The engine sizes each edict as `entityfields * 4` bytes of fields plus its own fixed header.
qcc counts one slot per non-vector field and three per vector field, in declaration order; a field's slot index is the count before it.
The engine does not check `entityfields` against the field definitions; `edicts.md` (P1-03) covers the system fields that must come first.
Loading a file that passes PROGS-3 yields every field of every record exactly as stored, after the little-endian conversion of PROGS-1.1; the loader changes no value.
Loading has no other effect on the file's contents: the tables keep their counts, order and duplicates, and the reserved first records stay as stored.
A file shorter than the 60-byte header is rejected.
A table whose offset or count is negative, or whose end (`offset + count * record size`) is past the end of the file, is rejected. The end is computed without overflow.
A string reference in a definition (`s_name`) or a function (`s_name`, `s_file`) that is negative or not less than `numstrings` is rejected.

A string reference whose bytes reach the end of the string table without a NUL is rejected. (id's engine would read on into the next table, or into the NUL that `COM_LoadFile` appends after the last byte of the file.)

A file is checked in this order and the first failure is reported: size, then version (PROGS-3.1), then header CRC (PROGS-3.2), then table bounds, then field definition flags (PROGS-3.4), then string references, then function parameter counts.
A function whose `numparms` is greater than 8 is rejected.

Statement opcodes and operands, function `first_statement`, `parm_start` and `locals`, definition `ofs`, and the values of globals are not checked at load, as in id's engine: what an out-of-range value does when executed is in `vm.md`.
A reader may skip the header CRC check (PROGS-3.2) when asked to, so the editor can open a mod whose system definitions differ from id's; the default is to check.

Within one step of PROGS-15.5 the first failure in this order is reported: table bounds in header order (statements, global definitions, field definitions, functions, strings, globals); field definitions in table order; string references of the global definitions, then of the field definitions, then of the functions, each in table order, with a function's `s_name` before its `s_file`; parameter counts in function order. id's engine has no such checks, so the order is ours; it follows the header and the loader's loops.
The type numbers used in definitions (PROGS-9.1) are:

The slot counts are id's `type_size` table. The engine computes the pointer's size as `sizeof(void *)/4`, which is 1 on the 32-bit x86 build id shipped and 2 on a 64-bit build; this spec fixes 1, the value of the shipped engine and of qcc's own table (`{1,1,1,3,1,1,1,1}`).

A definition type above 7 (after removing `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) is not a vanilla type. id's engine has no check for it and prints such a value as `bad type <n>`; a reader keeps the number rather than rejecting the file.
QuakeC has no way to declare a pointer: `ev_pointer` values exist only at run time, made by `OP_ADDRESS`, and qcc writes no definition of type 7.
A slot is 4 bytes read either as an f32 or as an i32; the engine reinterprets the same bits (`eval_t` is a union) and never converts between them when copying.
A string value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the string table (PROGS-11); 0 is the empty string.
A float value is the f32 in the slot; a vector is three consecutive float slots, x first.

An entity value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array, which is the entity number times the engine's edict size, not the entity number; 0 is the world. The file never holds a non-zero entity value, since QuakeC cannot initialise one.
A field value is an i32 slot index into an entity's fields (PROGS-13), so `.origin_y` is one more than `.origin`.
A function value is an i32 index into the functions table (PROGS-10); 0 is the null function.
A pointer value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array to one field slot of one entity.

Slot 0 is `OFS_NULL`; slots 1 to 3 hold a function's return value (`OFS_RETURN`, three slots so a vector fits); slots 4 to 27 hold the eight call parameters, three slots each, parameter `n` at `4 + 3n`.
Slots 0 to 27 have no global definitions in a file from qcc, and the system globals start at slot 28, which is why `progdefs.h` opens with `int pad[28]` (PROGS-5.1).
A version 7 file has a 92-byte header: the 60 bytes of PROGS-2, then eight more 4-byte fields:
`secondaryversion` 0x021B1461 (`"1FTE" ^ "PROG"` as little-endian i32) means the 16-bit layout of PROGS-7 and PROGS-9; 0x65167402 (`"1FTE" ^ "32B "`) means the 32-bit layout of PROGS-20.
FTE also accepts version 7 with `secondaryversion` `"UH27"` or `"KKQW"`, or any other value (treated as KKQWSV's format). Those are other engines' layouts; a reader rejects them as unsupported.
In FTE's header the offsets and counts are unsigned, but they are bounded by the file size, so PROGS-15.2 applies unchanged.
In the 16-bit layout FTE declares statement operands unsigned (`dstatement16_t`), so in a version 7 file the bytes `ff ff` are operand 65535. This differs from PROGS-7.2, which holds for version 6.
In the 32-bit layout a statement is 16 bytes: `op`, `a`, `b` and `c`, each a u32, at offsets 0, 4, 8 and 12.
In the 32-bit layout a definition is 12 bytes: `type` u32 at 0, `ofs` u32 at 4 and `s_name` i32 at 8. `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is still bit 15 of `type`.
Functions, strings and globals keep the layout of PROGS-10 to PROGS-12.
When `ofslinenums` is not 0, it is the offset of `numstatements` i32 source line numbers, one per statement in statement order.
The bodyless function table is `numbodylessfuncs` NUL-terminated names stored one after another from `ofsbodylessfuncs`.

Bit `n` of `blockscompressed` set means a table is stored compressed: bit 0 statements, 1 global definitions, 2 field definitions, 3 functions, 4 strings, 5 globals, 6 line numbers, 7 types. A compressed table starts at its offset with an i32 compressed length followed by that many bytes of zlib data (`QC_decode` method 2).

A reader rejects a file with any `blockscompressed` bit set, as FTE does when built without zlib; reading compressed tables would add a decompressor for a mode that FTEQCC's default settings do not produce (`compressoutput` is zero-initialised in `qccmain.c`).
`ofsfiles` and the type table carry no information the engine needs to run the program; a reader keeps their offsets and counts and does not decode them.
The version 7 header is followed by the same six tables as version 6, and PROGS-15 applies to them; opcodes above 65 and type numbers above 7 are FTE extensions that the vanilla VM does not execute.
When `ofsfiles` is not 0, it is the offset of an i32 count followed by that many 144-byte embedded file records (`includeddatafile_t`, read by `PR_TestRecompile`):

When `ofs_types` is not 0, it is the offset of `numtypes` 28-byte type records (`typeinfo_t`): seven i32 fields `type`, `next`, `aux_type`, `num_parms`, `ofs`, `size` and `name`, the last a string reference. FTEQCC at the pinned commit never writes the table (`types` is always false in `WriteData`).

A version 7 file is checked in this order, and the first failure is reported: a size of at least 60 bytes (PROGS-15.1), the version, a size of at least 92 bytes, the header CRC (PROGS-3.2, which PROGS-15.8 may skip), `secondaryversion` (PROGS-19.3), `blockscompressed` (PROGS-21.4), the bounds of the six tables (PROGS-15.9), the bounds of the line number table when `ofslinenums` is not 0 (`numstatements` 4-byte entries, as PROGS-15.2), the bodyless function names (every name's NUL inside the file, and a table of no names still at an offset no greater than the file size), then the remaining steps of PROGS-15.5. The embedded files and the type table are not checked (PROGS-21.5). FTE's loader checks none of the bounds, so the order is ours.

When no non-empty table overlaps another or the header, a file the reader accepts and the writer writes back unchanged is the same byte for byte: the writer places the non-empty tables in the order the file had them, with the bytes before, between and after them that the file had (PROGS-1.4), and gives each empty table the offset the file stored.

Without a source layout (a file built in memory, or one with overlapping tables) the writer uses qcc's order (PROGS-1.3): header, strings, statements, functions, global definitions, field definitions, globals, then for version 7 the line numbers and the bodyless function names. It pads the string table with NUL bytes to a multiple of 4 and `numstrings` counts the padding. An empty table's offset is where it would start, except that an empty bodyless function table has offset 0.

The writer computes every count and offset in the header from the tables, `version` and `secondaryversion` from the format, and writes `blockscompressed` as 0; `crc`, `entityfields`, `ofsfiles`, `ofs_types` and `numtypes` are written as given. With a source layout, a table the source did not have, or had empty, and that now has records goes after the source's last byte. A version 7 file with no line number table has `ofslinenums` 0.

The writer rejects a value that does not fit its field, with a typed error and no output: in version 6 an opcode above 65535, an operand outside -32768 to 32767, or a definition type or `ofs` above 65535; in the 16-bit version 7 layout also an operand outside 0 to 65535; a count or offset above 2147483647; a line number table whose length is not the number of statements; a bodyless function name containing a NUL; version 7 parts in a version 6 file; and `ofsfiles` or `ofs_types` other than 0 without a source layout, since the bytes they point at would not be kept.
When the records given to the writer pass the checks of PROGS-15, reading the written file gives back every record exactly as given.
A trace is one header (TRACE-2) followed by zero or more records (TRACE-4), in the order the events they describe happened. It has no end marker: it ends after its last complete record.
The binary form (TRACE-5) and the JSON form (TRACE-6) hold the same information. Decoding either form and encoding the result in the other, then decoding that, gives back the same header and records.

The header is written after the progs is loaded (its globals hold the values the file gives them) and before the first run. Every run the host starts after that is traced, including runs nested inside builtins (VM-18).

Globals are named by slot number, edicts by edict number (0 is the world) and entity fields by field slot number (PROGS-13), never by an address or an entity value, so the names do not depend on how a VM lays out its memory. Values are the raw 32-bit patterns of the slots (PROGS-17.1), written exactly, NaN payloads included.

The header holds the format version and five numbers: `progs_crc`, the CRC of the whole progs.dat file (PROGS-6.1, id's `pr_crc`), so a reader can check that two traces ran the same file; `edict_size`, the bytes between the entity values of consecutive edicts in this VM (id's `pr_edict_size`); `field_offset`, the bytes from an entity value to the pointer value of its field slot 0; `entityfields`, the number of field slots per edict (the progs header's `entityfields`); and `numstrings`, the size of the loaded string table in bytes.
The version is `TRACE_VERSION`. A reader rejects any other version: a change to the format that an old reader would misread is a new version.

`edict_size` is at least 1, `progs_crc` fits in 16 bits, and the fields fit inside an edict: `field_offset + 4 * entityfields` is at most `edict_size`, computed without overflow. A reader rejects a header that breaks any of these, and an emitter cannot write one.

A change set lists every global slot and every entity field slot whose 32-bit pattern, at the moment the record is written, differs from its pattern when the previous change-carrying record was written, or, for the first one, when the header was written. The patterns are compared as bits, so `-0.0` differs from `0.0` and a NaN equals itself only when its bits do.
Each slot appears at most once, with its value at the moment the record is written. A slot that changed and then changed back to its earlier pattern is not listed.
Global changes are in ascending order of slot. Field changes are in ascending order of edict number, and of field slot within one edict.

The globals compared are slots 0 to `numglobals - 1`. The fields compared are slots 0 to `entityfields - 1` of every edict the VM has in use (in id's engine edicts 0 to `sv.num_edicts - 1`), free or not. An edict that was not in use at the previous change-carrying record is compared against all-zero fields, so a newly allocated edict lists only its non-zero fields.

Only the globals and the fields are compared. The call stack, the local stack, the runaway counter, `pr_argc` and whether an edict is free are not in a change set; the differences they make show up in later globals and fields, or in the records' order.
